clinician.trajectory_summary: A 20-year-old female with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with sudden onset retrosternal chest pain radiating to the neck, associated with throat pain, dysphagia, voice change, and dyspnea exacerbated when supine. She denied preceding trauma, vomiting, foreign body ingestion, fever, cough, or recent procedures. On admission, she was vitally stable (HR 80, BP 108/55, RR 16, O2 sat 99% RA, temp 36.8°C) with epigastric tenderness on abdominal examination. Chest X-ray on admission revealed pneumomediastinum (E001). CT scan of the neck and chest showed retropharyngeal air extending to the mediastinum with anterior chest surgical emphysema and no foreign body (E002). Esophageal-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD) revealed mild gastritis with no evidence of esophageal injury or foreign body (E003). By the next day, the patient became vitally stable with complete resolution of pain and dyspnea (E004). Follow-up imaging one week post-discharge demonstrated complete resolution of retropharyngeal air and mediastinal emphysema with no fluid collections (E006). The clinical presentation, imaging findings of pneumomediastinum and retropharyngeal air extending to the mediastinum, and favorable clinical course with spontaneous resolution are consistent with spontaneous esophageal rupture managed conservatively.
